273	# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
274	# Non-tmux Tier 1: stdin / run / rerun sources
275	# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
276	# These three cover the "no tmux available" case (VSCode integrated terminal,
277	# bare Ghostty without tmux, quick SSH) by NOT relying on cpblock / OSC 133.
278	# Each composes zero magic — user explicitly picks the source.
279	#
280	# See backlog/ai-capture-non-tmux-output.md for why we don't do automatic
281	# tee redirection (Tier 2) or PTY proxy wrapping (Tier 3).
282	
283	# aifix-stdin: read whatever the caller piped in. Universal.
284	#   tail -200 /var/log/nginx/error.log | aifix-stdin
285	#   curl -sS https://weird.api/thing | aifix-stdin -p "explain this JSON"
286	#   aifix-stdin < build.log
287	aifix-stdin() {
288	  emulate -L zsh
289	  local name=aifix-stdin agent="" prompt_override="" raw=0 no_meta=0
290	  local default_prompt="Here is output captured from my terminal. Diagnose any errors and suggest a concrete fix. Be brief and specific."
291	  while (( $# )); do
292	    case "$1" in
293	      -a|--agent)   agent=$2; shift 2 ;;
294	      -p|--prompt)  prompt_override=$2; shift 2 ;;
295	      --raw)        raw=1; shift ;;
296	      --no-meta)    no_meta=1; shift ;;
297	      -h|--help)    _ai_print_help "$name" "[-a AGENT] [-p PROMPT] [--raw] [--no-meta]"
298	                    print -r -- "  Reads block from stdin. No tmux / cpblock dependency."
299	                    return 0 ;;
300	      *) print -u2 "$name: unexpected arg: $1 (did you mean -p?)"; return 1 ;;
301	    esac
302	  done
303	  if [[ -z "$agent" ]]; then
304	    agent=$(_aiagent_autodetect) || {
305	      print -u2 "$name: no coding-agent CLI found on PATH"
306	      return 1
307	    }
308	  fi
309	  # -t 0 checks if stdin is a terminal. If it is, user likely forgot to pipe.
310	  if [[ -t 0 ]]; then
311	    print -u2 "$name: stdin is a tty — did you forget to pipe? Example:"
312	    print -u2 "  some-command 2>&1 | $name"
313	    return 1
314	  fi
315	  local block
316	  block=$(cat)
317	  _ai_dispatch_core "$name" "stdin" "$default_prompt" \
318	    "$agent" "$raw" "$no_meta" "$prompt_override" "$block"
319	}
320	
321	# aifix-run: run CMD, tee stdout+stderr to a log, feed "$ CMD\n<output>\n(exit code: N)"
322	# to the agent. Use `--` to separate flags from the command.
323	#   aifix-run -- cargo build --release
324	#   aifix-run -p "is this safe?" -- ansible-playbook deploy.yml
325	#
326	# isatty caveat: teeing makes CMD's stdout a pipe, so TUI apps (vim, less)
327	# render in degraded mode. Don't use this for interactive tools.
328	aifix-run() {
329	  emulate -L zsh
330	  local name=aifix-run agent="" prompt_override="" raw=0 no_meta=0
331	  local default_prompt="Here is a command I ran in my terminal and its output. Diagnose any errors and suggest a concrete fix. Be brief and specific."
332	  while (( $# )); do
333	    case "$1" in
334	      -a|--agent)   agent=$2; shift 2 ;;
335	      -p|--prompt)  prompt_override=$2; shift 2 ;;
336	      --raw)        raw=1; shift ;;
337	      --no-meta)    no_meta=1; shift ;;
338	      -h|--help)    _ai_print_help "$name" "[-a AGENT] [-p PROMPT] [--raw] [--no-meta] -- CMD [ARG...]"
339	                    print -r -- "  Runs CMD with stdout+stderr teed to a log, feeds to agent."
340	                    print -r -- "  Use \`--\` to separate flags from the command."
341	                    return 0 ;;
342	      --) shift; break ;;
343	      -*) print -u2 "$name: unknown flag: $1"; return 1 ;;
344	      *) break ;;
345	    esac
346	  done
347	  if (( $# == 0 )); then
348	    print -u2 "$name: missing command. Usage: $name [flags] -- CMD [ARG...]"
349	    return 1
350	  fi
351	  if [[ -z "$agent" ]]; then
352	    agent=$(_aiagent_autodetect) || {
353	      print -u2 "$name: no coding-agent CLI found on PATH"
354	      return 1
355	    }
356	  fi
357	  local log
358	  log=$(mktemp -t aifix-run.XXXXXX) || { print -u2 "$name: mktemp failed"; return 1; }
359	  # Record the command line as the block's first line so the agent knows
360	  # what was run. Use $(print -r -- "$*") to preserve args verbatim.
361	  print -r -- "\$ $*" > "$log"
362	  "$@" 2>&1 | tee -a "$log"
363	  local rc=${pipestatus[1]}
364	  print -r -- "" >> "$log"
365	  print -r -- "(exit code: $rc)" >> "$log"
366	  local block
367	  block=$(<"$log")
368	  rm -f "$log"
369	  _ai_dispatch_core "$name" "run \`${1}…\` (exit $rc)" "$default_prompt" \
370	    "$agent" "$raw" "$no_meta" "$prompt_override" "$block"
371	}
372	
373	# aifix-rerun: thefuck-style. Re-executes the last command from shell history
374	# via aifix-run. Prompts for confirmation unless -y, because re-running has
375	# side effects if the command isn't idempotent.
376	aifix-rerun() {
377	  emulate -L zsh
378	  local name=aifix-rerun yes=0 forward=()
379	  while (( $# )); do
380	    case "$1" in
381	      -y|--yes) yes=1; shift ;;
382	      -h|--help) _ai_print_help "$name" "[-y] [-a AGENT] [-p PROMPT] [--raw] [--no-meta]"
383	                 print -r -- "  Re-executes the last command from zsh history via aifix-run."
384	                 print -r -- "  Prompts for confirmation unless -y (side effects beware)."
385	                 return 0 ;;
386	      *) forward+=("$1"); shift ;;
387	    esac
388	  done
389	  # fc -ln -2 -2: skip aifix-rerun itself (which is -1), grab the one before.
390	  local cmd
391	  cmd=$(fc -ln -2 -2 2>/dev/null)
392	  cmd="${cmd#	}"; cmd="${cmd# }"
393	  if [[ -z "$cmd" ]]; then
394	    print -u2 "$name: no prior command in shell history"
395	    return 1
396	  fi
397	  print -u2 "$name: will re-execute:"
398	  print -u2 "  $cmd"
399	  print -u2 "⚠ side effects if the command is not idempotent (network calls, file writes, etc.)"
400	  if (( ! yes )); then
401	    local reply
402	    read -q "reply?Proceed? [y/N] "
403	    print
404	    [[ "$reply" != "y" ]] && { print -u2 "$name: aborted"; return 130; }
405	  fi
406	  # Delegate to aifix-run via eval (preserves quoting for $cmd's shell syntax).
407	  eval "aifix-run ${forward[*]} -- $cmd"
408	}
409	
410	# aiblock — launch the Python TUI (scripts/aiblock.py) resolved via
411	# chezmoi source-path, cached per-shell. The Python side reads the same
412	# AICAP_* env vars so model defaults stay consistent.
413	#
414	# History passing: `fc -ln …` only works inside this interactive zsh —
415	# a `zsh -ic` subshell doesn't inherit the in-memory history buffer and
416	# `fc -R` only pulls whatever the HISTFILE has on disk (which misses
417	# unflushed recent commands). Dump the current shell's history into a
418	# temp file and hand the path to the TUI via $AIBLOCK_HIST_DUMP.
419	_AIBLOCK_SCRIPT=""
420	aiblock() {
421	  emulate -L zsh
422	  if [[ -z "$_AIBLOCK_SCRIPT" ]]; then
423	    local base
424	    base=$(chezmoi source-path 2>/dev/null) || {
425	      print -u2 "aiblock: could not resolve chezmoi source-path"
426	      return 1
427	    }
428	    _AIBLOCK_SCRIPT="$base/scripts/aiblock.py"
429	  fi
430	  if [[ ! -f "$_AIBLOCK_SCRIPT" ]]; then
431	    print -u2 "aiblock: $_AIBLOCK_SCRIPT not found (run 'chezmoi apply' after a git pull)"
432	    return 1
433	  fi
434	  local histdump
435	  histdump=$(mktemp -t aiblock-hist.XXXXXX) || {
436	    print -u2 "aiblock: mktemp failed"
437	    return 1
438	  }
439	  # fc -ln -30: last 30 entries, no numbering. Trailing newline per entry.
440	  fc -ln -30 > "$histdump" 2>/dev/null
441	  AIBLOCK_HIST_DUMP="$histdump" uv run --script "$_AIBLOCK_SCRIPT" "$@"
442	  local rc=$?
443	  rm -f "$histdump"
444	  return $rc
445	}

1	# aisuggest — prompt-time NL→shell ghost text via the existing _aiagent_invoke
2	# layer. Press the trigger (Alt+; default) to translate the current BUFFER from
3	# natural language into a single shell command, shown as ghost text. Tab or →
4	# accepts; any other keypress dismisses.

6	# Integrates with 04_ai_capture.zsh (_aiagent_invoke / _aiagent_autodetect) so
7	# the same agent autodetect (claude → opencode → codex → cursor-agent) and the
8	# same AICAP_*_MODEL defaults apply. No API key needed when claude / opencode /
9	# codex / cursor-agent CLIs are authenticated.
10	#
11	# Env-var defaults (set in ~/.zshrc.adhoc or ~/.config/zsh/secrets.zsh to
12	# override; do not edit this file):
13	#
14	#   AISUGGEST_KEY              default: ^[;            (Alt+;)
15	#   AISUGGEST_AGENT            default: empty          (autodetect at invoke)
16	#   AISUGGEST_MODEL            default: empty          (use AICAP_*_MODEL)
17	#   AISUGGEST_HIGHLIGHT        default: fg=8           (region_highlight style)
18	#   AISUGGEST_PROMPT_OVERRIDE  default: empty          (replace built-in prompt)

20	#                                                       to $AISUGGEST_LOG;
21	#                                                       runtime-toggleable)
22	#   AISUGGEST_LOG              default: /tmp/aisuggest.log
23	#
24	# Debugging:
25	#   `aisuggest "<text>"`              CLI form — same pipeline as the widget,
26	#                                     prints the suggestion to stdout.

28	#                                     stderr layer-by-layer.

34	#   1. Low-latency claude flag profile — bypass _aiagent_invoke for `agent==claude`,
35	#      shell out with `--no-session-persistence --effort low --no-chrome --tools ""
36	#      --setting-sources "" --system-prompt "$sys" "$user_input"`. ~1.5x faster.
37	#      Upstream ref: providers/claude-code.zsh.

41	#      A non-blocking flow (background agent → FD watcher → render-on-arrival) lets
42	#      the user keep typing while the suggestion renders.

44	#      without any of the four CLIs installed. Pair with a key-retrieval-command

47	#      control-char payloads → assert _aisuggest_sanitize strips them).
48	#   6. Per-agent model env vars (AISUGGEST_CLAUDE_MODEL, AISUGGEST_OPENCODE_MODEL, …)

117	# ============================================================================
118	# Sanitize model output (security boundary)
119	# ============================================================================
120	# Strip ANSI escape sequences and control characters before they touch BUFFER
121	# or POSTDISPLAY. A model that emits crafted escapes could otherwise overwrite
122	# what we display.
123	_aisuggest_sanitize() {
124	  setopt local_options extended_glob
125	  local input=$1
126	  local sanitized=$input
127	  local esc=$'\x1b'
128	  while [[ $sanitized == *${esc}\[* ]]; do
129	    sanitized=${sanitized//${esc}\[[0-9;]#[A-Za-z]/}
130	  done
131	  sanitized=${sanitized//${esc}/}
132	  sanitized=${sanitized//[$'\x00'-$'\x08'$'\x0a'-$'\x1f'$'\x7f']/}
133	  sanitized=${sanitized##[[:space:]]##}
134	  sanitized=${sanitized%%[[:space:]]##}
135	  print -r -- "$sanitized"
136	}

138	_aisuggest_log() {
139	  (( AISUGGEST_DEBUG )) || return 0

146	_aisuggest_query() {

149

154	    else

157	  fi
158	
159	  local sys_prompt="${AISUGGEST_PROMPT_OVERRIDE:-$_AISUGGEST_BUILTIN_PROMPT}"
160	  local context="<context>
161	OS: $_AISUGGEST_OS
162	Shell: ${SHELL:t}
163	PWD: $PWD
164	</context>"
165	
166	  # _aiagent_invoke takes one prompt arg; concatenate system + context + user.
167	  local prompt="${sys_prompt}
168	
169	${context}
170	
171	User: ${user_input}"
172	
173	  _aisuggest_log "agent=$agent input=$user_input"
174	
175	  # Optionally pin model. AICAP_*_MODEL is per-agent (see 04_ai_capture.zsh).
176	  local saved_claude=$AICAP_CLAUDE_MODEL
177	  local saved_opencode=$AICAP_OPENCODE_MODEL
178	  local saved_codex=$AICAP_CODEX_MODEL
179	  local saved_cursor=$AICAP_CURSOR_MODEL
180	  if [[ -n $AISUGGEST_MODEL ]]; then
181	    case $agent in
182	      claude)       AICAP_CLAUDE_MODEL=$AISUGGEST_MODEL ;;
183	      opencode)     AICAP_OPENCODE_MODEL=$AISUGGEST_MODEL ;;
184	      codex)        AICAP_CODEX_MODEL=$AISUGGEST_MODEL ;;
185	      cursor-agent) AICAP_CURSOR_MODEL=$AISUGGEST_MODEL ;;
186	    esac
187	  fi
188	
189	  local reply
190	  reply=$(AICAP_SHOW_METADATA=0 AICAP_SPINNER=0 AICAP_PRETTIFY=0 \
191	          _aiagent_invoke "$agent" "$prompt" 2>/dev/null)
192	  local rc=$?
193	
194	  AICAP_CLAUDE_MODEL=$saved_claude
195	  AICAP_OPENCODE_MODEL=$saved_opencode
196	  AICAP_CODEX_MODEL=$saved_codex
197	  AICAP_CURSOR_MODEL=$saved_cursor

199	  (( rc != 0 )) && { _aisuggest_log "agent failed rc=$rc"; return $rc; }
200	
201	  # Post-filter: keep first non-blank line, strip leading $/# prompt markers,
202	  # strip surrounding backticks/fences. Defensive against models that ignore
203	  # the system-prompt instructions.
204	  reply=$(print -r -- "$reply" \
205	          | awk 'NF { print; exit }' \
206	          | sed -E 's/^[[:space:]]*[#$][[:space:]]*//' \
207	          | sed -E 's/^`+//; s/`+$//' \
208	          | sed -E 's/^```[a-z]*//' )

210	  print -r -- "$reply"
211	}

216	_aisuggest_show_ghost() {
217	  local suggestion=$1
218	
219	  # Clear our previous highlight (if any) — match by exact entry so we don't
220	  # touch other plugins' (zsh-syntax-highlighting, etc).

248	# On activate: snapshot Tab and right-arrow bindings, then swap them for our

250	_aisuggest_activate() {

261	  bindkey '^[[C' _aisuggest_accept_right

266	_aisuggest_deactivate() {

294	# Pre-redraw: if buffer changed, decide whether to keep the suggestion (still

315	# Line-finish: deactivate before line submission so Tab/→ are restored before

322	# Main widget — Alt+; (or AISUGGEST_KEY) requests a suggestion

324	_aisuggest_widget() {

356	  wait $pid 2>/dev/null

361	  [[ -f "${tmpfile}.err" ]] && raw_err=$(<"${tmpfile}.err")

364	  [[ -n $raw_err ]] && _aisuggest_log "widget: raw stderr=[$raw_err]"

372	    _aisuggest_show_ghost "$suggestion"

375	    _aisuggest_log "widget: rendered ghost, activated"

377	    POSTDISPLAY=""
378	    zle -M "aisuggest: no suggestion"
379	    _aisuggest_log "widget: empty suggestion → 'no suggestion' branch"
380	  fi

383	# ============================================================================
384	# Accept handlers (only intercept while active; fall through to original)

471	suggested command to stdout. Use this to debug widget issues without ZLE
472	in the picture.

474	  aisuggest "find files larger than 100 MB"
475	  aisuggest --debug "list 10 largest files in cwd"

477	Env (see docs/tools/zsh-inline-ai.md):

479	  AISUGGEST_MODEL=<model>                                     pin model

505	  local context="<context>

507	Shell: ${SHELL:t}
508	PWD: $PWD
509	</context>"
510	  local full_prompt="${sys_prompt}
511	
512	${context}
513	
514	User: ${input}"
515	
516	  {
517	    print -- "----- aisuggest --debug -----"
518	    print -- "agent:                $agent"
519	    print -- "AISUGGEST_KEY:        $AISUGGEST_KEY"
520	    print -- "AISUGGEST_AGENT:      ${AISUGGEST_AGENT:-<unset; autodetected>}"

528	    print -- "context:              $context"
529	    print -- "----- invoking _aiagent_invoke (rc + raw stdout below; stderr next) -----"

532	  local raw stderr_log
533	  stderr_log=$(mktemp -t aisuggest.err.XXXXXX) || return 1

542	    cat "$stderr_log"

546	  local sanitized

549	  print -ru2 -- "$sanitized"

1	# 11_tools_picker.zsh - Interactive CLI tools picker (fzf ZLE widget)
2	# Reads ~/.config/docs/tools/cli-tools.md for the tool list (deployed by chezmoi).
3	#
4	# Alt+T  →  open picker
5	#   Enter      paste invocation to shell buffer (you still press Enter to run)
6	#   Ctrl+E     execute the tool directly (good for TUI apps: btop, lazygit, etc.)
7	#   Ctrl+/     toggle preview panel (shows tldr or --help)
8	#
9	# The invocation for tools that need arguments has a trailing space,
10	# so pressing Enter pastes e.g. "rg " — cursor lands after the space,
11	# ready for you to type your arguments.
12	
13	_TOOLS_DOC="${HOME}/.config/docs/tools/cli-tools.md"
14	
15	# Bail silently if the data file hasn't been deployed yet or fzf is missing
16	[[ -f "$_TOOLS_DOC" ]] || return 0
17	command -v fzf &>/dev/null || return 0
18	
19	# Parse the markdown tables into "INVOCATION<TAB>DESCRIPTION" lines.
20	# Tab separator preserves the trailing space in invocations like "rg ".
21	_tools_list() {
22	    awk -F'|' '/^[[:space:]]*\|[[:space:]]*`/ {
23	      inv=$3; sub(/^[[:space:]]*`/,"",inv); sub(/`[[:space:]]*$/,"",inv)
24	      desc=$4; sub(/^[[:space:]]*/,"",desc); sub(/[[:space:]]*$/,"",desc)
25	      printf "%s\t%s\n", inv, desc
26	    }' "$_TOOLS_DOC"
27	}
28	
29	# ZLE widget: opens fzf picker, pastes selected invocation to the shell command line.
30	tools-picker() {
31	    {
32	        exec </dev/tty
33	        exec <&1
34	
35	        local selected
36	        selected=$(
37	            _tools_list | fzf \
38	                --ansi \
39	                --border \
40	                --prompt ' tools  ' \
41	                --header 'Enter: paste  Ctrl+E: execute  Ctrl+/: preview' \
42	                --delimiter=$'\t' \
43	                --with-nth=1,2 \
44	                --preview 'tool=$(printf "%s" {1} | awk "{print \$1}" | sed "s/ *$//"); (command -v tldr >/dev/null 2>&1 && tldr "$tool" 2>/dev/null) || "$tool" --help 2>&1 | head -50' \
45	                --preview-window='right:55%:wrap:hidden' \
46	                --bind='ctrl-/:toggle-preview' \
47	                --bind='ctrl-e:execute(eval $(printf "%s" {1} | awk "{print \$1}"))+abort'
48	        )
49	
50	        zle reset-prompt >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
51	        [[ -z "$selected" ]] && return
52	
53	        # Extract the invocation (field 1 before the tab), preserving trailing space
54	        local invocation
55	        invocation=$(printf '%s' "$selected" | cut -f1)
56	
57	        # Paste to shell command line buffer without executing
58	        LBUFFER="${LBUFFER}${invocation}"
59	        zle redisplay
60	    }
61	}
62

64

67	bindkey -M emacs '\et' tools-picker
68	bindkey -M viins '\et' tools-picker
69	bindkey -M vicmd '\et' tools-picker

377	# ── svibe: parametric multi-agent vibe layout ───────────────────────────────

379	# A "vibe coding" session: window 1 has N agent panes (default 4), window 2
380	# is lazygit, window 3 is nvim. Built directly with tmux split/new-window
381	# commands so it stays parametric (tmuxp YAML can't express dynamic pane counts).
382	#

384	# Refuses outside a git repo (use `shere` for plain shells in arbitrary dirs).
385	#

389	# keeps the pane open with a hint after the agent exits, so Ctrl+C is
390	# recoverable.
391	#
392	# Two modes for choosing which agents run:
393	#   1. Homogeneous (positional): `svibe 4 codex` → 4 panes all running codex
394	#   2. Heterogeneous (--agents):  `svibe --agents claude,codex,codex,opencode`
395	#                                 → 4 panes running those specific agents
396	#                                 (list LENGTH determines pane count;
397	#                                 positional N_AGENTS is rejected to avoid
398	#                                 ambiguity)
399	#
400	# Usage:
401	#   svibe                                          # 4× claude (specstory)
402	#   svibe 2                                        # 2× claude
403	#   svibe 4 codex                                  # 4× specstory run codex
404	#   svibe 3 opencode                               # 3× opencode (raw)
405	#   svibe --agents claude,codex,codex,opencode     # 4 panes, mixed
406	#   svibe --agents claude,opencode --on-exit kill  # 2 panes, mixed, hard exit
407	#   svibe --no-specstory 4 claude                  # 4× claude (raw, no md auto-save)
408	#   svibe --on-exit restart 4 codex                # auto-respawn loop
409	#   svibe -p ~/repo 4 claude                       # explicit path
410	#   svibe --no-attach 4 claude                     # create in background
411	function sesh-vibe() {
412	    local target="" no_attach=0 on_exit="shell" specstory_mode="auto"
413	    local n_agents=4 n_agents_set=0
414	    local agent_cli="claude"
415	    local agents_csv=""
416	    local min_width="${SVIBE_MIN_WIDTH:-80}"

422	            --min-width)    min_width="$2"; shift 2 ;;
423	            --no-specstory) specstory_mode="never"; shift ;;
424	            --specstory)    specstory_mode="auto"; shift ;;

430	Usage:
431	  svibe [--path DIR] [--on-exit MODE] [--no-specstory] [--no-attach]
432	        [--min-width COLS] [N_AGENTS] [AGENT_CLI]
433	  svibe [--path DIR] [--on-exit MODE] [--no-specstory] [--no-attach]
434	        [--min-width COLS] --agents A1,A2,A3[,...]
435	
436	Default: svibe           (N auto-picked from term_width ÷ min-width, clamp [1,12])
437	  window 1 "agents" — N agent panes (columns if all fit at ≥min-width, else tiled)
438	  window 2 "git"    — lazygit

440	
441	Two modes for choosing agents:

445

451	  opencode (and other unknown CLIs)         → raw passthrough
452	
453	--on-exit MODE controls per-pane behavior on Ctrl+C / clean exit
454	(applies to all agent panes, the lazygit window, and the nvim window):
455	  shell    (default) — drop to shell with a hint, command re-runnable
456	  kill                — let the pane/window close (tmux default)
457	  restart             — auto-respawn the command in a loop
458	
459	--min-width COLS sets the minimum readable per-pane width (default: value of
460	$SVIBE_MIN_WIDTH, else 80). It drives two decisions:
461	  • auto-pick N when you don't pass a count (N = term_width / min-width)
462	  • columns vs tiled in the agents window: columns when all N panes fit at
463	    ≥COLS wide side-by-side, otherwise tiled grid
464	Example on a 240-col terminal:
465	  min-width 80   → auto N=3, three even-horizontal columns
466	  min-width 120  → auto N=2, two even-horizontal columns
467	
468	Examples:
469	  svibe                                            # auto N × claude, width-aware layout
470	  svibe 2                                          # 2× claude
471	  svibe 4 codex                                    # 4× codex
472	  svibe 6 opencode                                 # 6× opencode (heavy)
473	  svibe --min-width 120                            # wider panes → fewer auto columns
474	  svibe --agents claude,codex,codex,opencode       # 4 panes, mixed

476	  svibe --no-specstory 4 claude                    # raw claude, no auto-save
477	EOF

## Collision Risk & Safe-Merge Options: Managed ~/.bashrc in Chezmoi

This write-up addresses the risk of clobbering stock `~/.bashrc` across distributions and outlines safe merge patterns for a chezmoi-managed bashrc that preserves distro defaults while adding custom configuration.

### 1. Stock `~/.bashrc` across Distributions

#### **Ubuntu 22.04 / 24.04** (`/etc/skel/.bashrc`)

The skeleton file includes these load-bearing blocks (verbatim structure, not exhaustive):

**Early-return guard for non-interactive shells:**
```bash
# If not running interactively, don't do anything
[[ $- != *i* ]] && return
```
This is critical: any code after this guard will never run in non-interactive shells (SSH commands, cron jobs, etc.). Your managed bashrc must preserve this pattern if you add environment variables that need to propagate to non-interactive contexts.

**History settings:**
```bash
HISTCONTROL=ignoreboth     # Ignore duplicate lines + lines starting with space
HISTSIZE=1000
HISTFILESIZE=2000
shopt -s histappend         # Append to history file, don't overwrite
```
**Status:** REPLACE. These are reasonable defaults but you likely want larger history (e.g., 10000+). Safe to override.

**Shell options:**
```bash
shopt -s checkwinsize       # Update LINES/COLUMNS after each command
# shopt -s globstar          # Enable ** pathname expansion (commented out)
```
**Status:** PRESERVE for `checkwinsize`; decide independently on `globstar` (harmless, some find useful).

**Prompt & color aliases:**
```bash
if [ -z "${debian_chroot:-}" ] && [ -r /etc/debian_chroot ]; then
    debian_chroot=$(cat /etc/debian_chroot)
fi
PS1='${debian_chroot:+($debian_chroot)}\u@\h:\w\$ '

# Enable color support for ls
if [ -x /usr/bin/dircolors ]; then
    test -r ~/.dircolors && eval "$(dircolors -b ~/.dircolors)" || eval "$(dircolors -b)"
    alias ls='ls --color=auto'
    alias grep='grep --color=auto'
fi

# colored GCC warnings and errors
export GCC_COLORS='error=01;31:warning=01;35:note=01;36:caret=01;32:locus=01:quote=01'
```
**Status:** CONFLICT-AWARE. Your managed bashrc uses `starship` for PS1, so the debian_chroot/TERM-based prompt is removed. The `dircolors` aliases and `GCC_COLORS` are harmless to preserve if desired, but not essential if you handle color separately.

**Bash completion & aliases sourcing:**
```bash
[ -r ~/.bash_aliases ] && . ~/.bash_aliases
if ! shopt -oq posix; then
    if [ -f /usr/share/bash-completion/bash_completion ]; then
        . /usr/share/bash-completion/bash_completion
    elif [ -f /etc/bash_completion ]; then
        . /etc/bash_completion
    fi
fi
```
**Status:** PRESERVE structure. This is how you'd source `oh-my-bash.sh` if using OMB, or your own modular `~/.config/bash/` subdirs (parallel to the zshrc pattern you already use).

#### **Debian 12 (Bookworm)**

Identical to Ubuntu in structure (both derived from the GNU bash skeleton). Key difference: Debian's `/etc/bashrc` is typically minimal; the real config is in `/etc/skel/.bashrc`. **No surprising divergence.**

#### **Fedora / Rocky Linux 9** (`/etc/skel/.bashrc` + `/etc/bashrc`)

**User `.bashrc` delegates to system:**
```bash
# .bashrc
# Source global definitions
if [ -f /etc/bashrc ]; then
    . /etc/bashrc
fi
# User specific aliases and functions
```

**System `/etc/bashrc` includes:**
- Module system integration (module load commands)
- Prompt color detection
- Alias definitions for `rm -i`, `cp -i`, `mv -i` (dangerous-operation guards)
- History settings (often inherited)

**Status:** CRITICAL DIFFERENCE. On RHEL-family systems, the stack is: user `~/.bashrc` → `/etc/bashrc` → `/etc/profile.d/*.sh`. If your managed bashrc doesn't source `/etc/bashrc`, you lose the system's protective aliases and module environment. Safe pattern:
```bash
[[ $- != *i* ]] && return  # Non-interactive early exit
if [ -f /etc/bashrc ]; then
    . /etc/bashrc
fi
# Your config here
```

#### **macOS**

**No stock `~/.bashrc` by default.** Bash is 3.2.57 (GPLv3 license reluctance; not updated since 2009). macOS login shells read `~/.bash_profile`, not `~/.bashrc`.

**Homebrew-installed bash (6.x+) reads the same order as Linux.** But if the user has `/opt/homebrew/bin/bash` as their shell and you deploy `~/.bashrc`, they must have `~/.bash_profile` source it. Quote from your own zshrc pattern:

```bash
{{ if eq .chezmoi.os "darwin" -}}
if [[ -f /opt/homebrew/bin/brew ]]; then
    eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"
elif [[ -f /usr/local/bin/brew ]]; then
    eval "$(/usr/local/bin/brew shellenv)"
fi
{{ end -}}
```

**Status:** On macOS, you must also manage `~/.bash_profile` (or detect and skip bashrc deployment if no Homebrew bash). The default empty state means zero collision risk, but also zero baseline to preserve.

#### **WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux)**

WSL uses the same distro skeleton as its base (e.g., Ubuntu 22.04 in WSL is identical to baremetal Ubuntu). No special handling needed; treat as Ubuntu/Debian.

---

### 2. `~/.bash_profile` / `~/.profile` / `~/.bash_login` Ordering

**Canonical bash man page (INVOCATION → login shell):**

> "If the shell is invoked as a login shell, or as a non-interactive shell with the `--login` option, it first reads and executes commands from the file `/etc/profile`, if that file exists. After reading that file, it looks for `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login`, and `~/.profile`, in that order, and reads and executes commands from the first one that exists and is readable."

**Key implication:** Only the **first found** file is sourced. If you have `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login` is ignored, and `~/.profile` is ignored.

**Best practice pattern (Ubuntu/Debian default in `/etc/skel/.bash_profile`):**
```bash
if [ -n "$BASH_VERSION" ]; then
    if [ -f "$HOME/.bashrc" ]; then
        . "$HOME/.bashrc"
    fi
fi
```

This ensures that login shells get bashrc settings without duplication. **macOS caveat:** If using Homebrew bash and managing both files via chezmoi, put the sourcing logic in `~/.bash_profile` (login shells) and keep `~/.bashrc` for interactive shells. Do not put them in `~/.profile` alone, or standard bash won't read them on macOS.

---

### 3. Existing Chezmoi Patterns: How `dot_zshrc.tmpl` Avoids Collision

Your `dot_zshrc.tmpl` provides the gold standard for wrap-not-replace:

1. **Preserves stock oh-my-zsh:** Doesn't replace `/etc/skel/.zshrc`; instead, sources oh-my-zsh explicitly:
   ```bash
   [[ -f "$ZSH/oh-my-zsh.sh" ]] && source "$ZSH/oh-my-zsh.sh"
   ```

2. **Modular config loader:** Rather than inlining everything, it has a pattern-applied directory loader:
   ```bash
   load_zsh_dir() {
       local dir="$1"
       [[ -d "$dir" ]] || return 0
       setopt local_options null_glob
       local f
       for f in "$dir"/*.zsh; do
           [[ -r "$f" ]] && source "$f"
       done
   }
   load_zsh_dir "$ZSH_CONFIG_DIR/tools"
   ```
   This allows users to drop new files in `~/.config/zsh/tools/` without editing the main config.

3. **Adhoc escape hatch:** The `.zshrc.adhoc` file (sourced at the end, unchecked) allows machine-specific overrides without touching chezmoi. You explicitly create it if missing and source it:
   ```bash
   [[ -r "$HOME/.zshrc.adhoc" ]] && source "$HOME/.zshrc.adhoc"
   ```

4. **Ignore list:** `.chezmoiignore.tmpl` excludes `.zshrc.adhoc` so it never gets overwritten:
   ```
   # Zsh adhoc file (personal experiments - never track)
   .zshrc.adhoc
   ```

**Recommendation for bashrc:** Mirror this exactly. Create `dot_bashrc.tmpl` that:
- Sources `/etc/bashrc` (RHEL) or `/usr/share/bash-completion/bash_completion` (Debian/Ubuntu) at the top
- Loads a modular `~/.config/bash/` directory (instead of inline config)
- Has a `.bashrc.adhoc` escape hatch
- Respects the early-return guard and never puts env vars after it (move them to `~/.bash_env` or `.bash_profile`)

---

### 4. Oh-My-Bash Installation Footprint

From the install.sh script analysis:

**Installation location:** `~/.oh-my-bash/` (hardcoded, not configurable).

**Backup on collision:**
```bash
local bashrc_backup=~/.bashrc.omb-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)
printf '%s\\n' "${YELLOW}Found ~/.bashrc.${NORMAL} ${GREEN}Backing up to $bashrc_backup${NORMAL}"
_omb_install_run mv ~/.bashrc "$bashrc_backup"
```
It **moves** (not copies) the existing `~/.bashrc` to a timestamped backup, then writes a new one. This is destructive if you're not paying attention, but gives you a dated backup.

**Unattended install flag:**
```bash
bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ohmybash/oh-my-bash/master/tools/install.sh)" --unattended
```
The `--unattended` flag prevents the installer from changing your default shell (`chsh`) and exiting the shell after install. **No `--keep-bashrc` flag exists;** you must manually preserve your bashrc before running the installer or be comfortable with `.omb-backup-*`.

**New `.bashrc` template:**
```bash
export OSH="$HOME/.oh-my-bash"
[[ "$OSTYPE" == "darwin"* ]] && OSH="$HOME/.oh-my-bash"
export THEME="powerline"     # Can be customized
export COMPLETION_WAITING_DOTS="true"
source "$OSH/oh-my-bash.sh"
```
It's minimal; your custom config would go below.

**Footgun: Theme conflicts.** If OMB's theme is enabled (e.g., "powerline"), it will fight with starship. You'd need to set `THEME=""` and then source starship *after* OMB loads.

**Footgun: bash-preexec dependency.** Oh-My-Bash can install bash-preexec as a plugin. This can conflict with starship's internal preexec handling if not ordered carefully (see section 6 below).

**Recommendation:** If using oh-my-bash with chezmoi, gate it conditionally:
```bash
if [[ -d ~/.oh-my-bash ]]; then
    export OSH="$HOME/.oh-my-bash"
    export THEME=""  # Disable OMB theme, use starship instead
    source "$OSH/oh-my-bash.sh"
fi
```

---

### 5. ble.sh Interaction Story

From the ble.sh README:

**Stable installation methods:**
1. **Source build:** `git clone --recursive && make -C ble.sh install PREFIX=~/.local`
2. **Nightly tarball:** `curl -L ... | tar xJf -`
3. **Package managers:** AUR (blesh-git), NixOS, Guix

**Startup pattern:**
```bash
[[ $- == *i* ]] && source -- /path/to/blesh/ble.sh --attach=none
[[ ! ${BLE_VERSION-} ]] || ble-attach
```
The `--attach=none` delays attachment until you explicitly call `ble-attach`, avoiding conflicts.

**Known compatibility:** The README states ble.sh can coexist with bash-it and oh-my-bash, but offers **no specific detail about starship or bash-preexec.** This is a concern: ble.sh is a complex line editor that may hook the same bash traps as starship. 

**Startup time:** ble.sh adds ~100–200ms to startup on first load (caches thereafter). On a ~2ms bash startup, this is noticeable.

**Integration with this bashrc:** Deferring ble.sh for v2. Reason: it requires careful initialization order (after starship, before user aliases), and its term-specific behavior may surprise users. Document it as optional: users can add ble.sh to `.bashrc.adhoc` and test compatibility.

---

### 6. `/etc/bash_completion` vs `bash-completion@2` (Homebrew)

**Linux default:** `/etc/bash_completion` (shell script, provided by the `bash-completion` package).

**Homebrew macOS:** Installs `bash-completion@2` to:
- Intel Macs: `/usr/local/etc/bash_completion.d/`, sourced from `/usr/local/etc/profile.d/bash_completion.sh`
- Apple Silicon: `/opt/homebrew/etc/bash_completion.d/`, sourced from `/opt/homebrew/etc/profile.d/bash_completion.sh`

**The problem:** Hardcoding `/usr/local` breaks on Apple Silicon. The solution (from Homebrew docs):

```bash
if type brew &>/dev/null; then
    HOMEBREW_PREFIX="$(brew --prefix)"
    if [[ -r "${HOMEBREW_PREFIX}/etc/profile.d/bash_completion.sh" ]]; then
        source "${HOMEBREW_PREFIX}/etc/profile.d/bash_completion.sh"
    fi
fi
```

This dynamically detects the prefix. On non-macOS systems, the `type brew` check short-circuits.

**Your managed bashrc should include this in a `~/.config/bash/` module** (e.g., `10_completion.bash`), keeping the main bashrc lean.

---

### 7. `$SHELL` Environment Variable vs Login Shell Mismatch

**The problem:** After running `chsh -s /opt/homebrew/bin/bash`, the shell is changed in `/etc/passwd`, but the `$SHELL` environment variable may still point to the old shell until you log out and log back in.

**Failure modes:**

1. **Starship init issue:** Starship usually doesn't care (it detects the running shell, not `$SHELL`), but if any part of your config reads `$SHELL` to conditionally enable features, mismatch causes weirdness.

2. **Atuin integration:** Atuin may use `$SHELL` to determine which shell hooks to load. If `$SHELL=/bin/zsh` but you're running `/opt/homebrew/bin/bash`, atuin might not initialize.

3. **Subshell spawning:** If a script or tool does `$SHELL -c "..."`, it spawns the wrong shell if `$SHELL` is stale.

4. **Non-standard shell paths:** Some tools check `/etc/shells` to validate shell paths. On macOS, Homebrew-installed bash (e.g., `/opt/homebrew/bin/bash`) is not in `/etc/shells` by default, and `chsh` will refuse it.

**Mitigation:**
- Document that users must run `chsh -s /opt/homebrew/bin/bash` and then log out/in to update `$SHELL`.
- On macOS, first run `echo /opt/homebrew/bin/bash | sudo tee -a /etc/shells` to whitelist the path.
- Optionally, add a post-apply hook in chezmoi to detect and warn: "bash_profile found but $SHELL still points to zsh; please log out and back in."

**For your bashrc, avoid reading `$SHELL`; always use `${BASH_VERSION-}` to detect if bash is running.**

---

### Summary: Safe Merge Strategy for Chezmoi-Managed `.bashrc`

1. **Don't replace; source.** Keep the early-return guard (`[[ $- != *i* ]] && return`). Source `/etc/bashrc` or `/usr/share/bash-completion/bash_completion` at the top.

2. **Modular loading.** Use the pattern from `dot_zshrc.tmpl`: load `~/.config/bash/*.bash` files (sorted). This keeps the main bashrc minimal and user-extensible.

3. **Distro conditionals.** In `.chezmoidata.toml` or `.chezmoi.json`, gate oh-my-bash and bash-completion setup on OS and whether the tool is installed.

4. **Adhoc escape hatch.** Create `~/.bashrc.adhoc` on first apply (like zshrc does), source it at the end, and add it to `.chezmoiignore.tmpl` so users can override without merge conflicts.

5. **Login shell sourcing.** Manage `~/.bash_profile` (or `~/.profile`) separately to source `~/.bashrc` and handle Homebrew bash on macOS.

6. **oh-my-bash conditional.** If OMB is installed, set `THEME=""` and coordinate with starship. Document that OMB's installer will back up your bashrc to `.omb-backup-*`, so be aware if you re-run it.

7. **Document the caveat:** macOS has no default bashrc, so new users won't collide. Linux users upgrading an existing `/etc/skel/.bashrc` should review the diff; chezmoi's apply workflow will show the collision and ask before overwriting.

## Key Design Patterns for Your Feature

**Prompt integration checklist for adding `primaryShell` choice:**

1. **`.chezmoi.toml.tmpl`** (after line 26):
   ```go
   {{- $primaryShell := promptChoiceOnce . "primaryShell" "Primary interactive shell" (list "zsh" "bash") "zsh" }}

2. **`scripts/init/dotfiles_init.py` PROMPTS tuple** (add after email/name, before feature groups):
   ```python

          "Which shell for interactive login (zsh provides advanced config).",
          default="zsh",
          prompt_text="Primary interactive shell",
          choices=("zsh", "bash"),
          hidden=True),  # if it's a basic, or False if in feature groups
   ```

3. **`Dockerfile` ARG block** (add after CHEZMOI_PROFILE):
   ```dockerfile
   ARG CHEZMOI_PRIMARY_SHELL=zsh
   ```

4. **`Dockerfile` chezmoi init flags** (add to line 127 region):
   ```dockerfile
   --promptChoice "Primary interactive shell=${CHEZMOI_PRIMARY_SHELL}" \
   ```

5. **Run `doctor` to verify parity:**
   ```bash
   uv run --script scripts/init/dotfiles_init.py doctor
   ```

6. **Gate zsh file deployment** via templates:
   - `{{ if eq .primaryShell "zsh" }} ... {{ end }}`
   - Wrap `dot_zshrc.tmpl`, `dot_config/zsh/**` with the condition
   - Create `dot_bashrc.tmpl`, `dot_config/bash/**` and gate to `{{ if eq .primaryShell "bash" }}`

# ble.sh Installation & Compatibility

## Installation Methods

**ble.sh** offers three primary installation approaches:

1. **From Source** - Clone the git repository and build using `make`:
   ```bash
   git clone --recursive --depth 1 --shallow-submodules https://github.com/akinomyoga/ble.sh.git
   make -C ble.sh install PREFIX=~/.local
   ```

2. **Nightly Build** - Download pre-built tarball via `curl` or `wget`:
   ```bash
   curl -L https://github.com/akinomyoga/ble.sh/releases/download/nightly/ble-nightly.tar.xz | tar xJf -
   ```

3. **Package Managers** - Available through AUR (`blesh-git`), NixOS, and Guix.

After installation, add to `~/.bashrc`:
```bash
[[ $- == *i* ]] && source -- /path/to/blesh/ble.sh --attach=none
[[ ! ${BLE_VERSION-} ]] || ble-attach
```

## Compatibility Notes

The documentation mentions that "ble.sh can be used in combination with other Bash configurations such as bash-it and oh-my-bash," indicating general compatibility with these frameworks.

However, **no specific details about starship or bash-preexec compatibility appear in the provided documentation**. For fzf integration specifically, the guide recommends consulting the dedicated contrib repository to avoid compatibility issues.

The search results provide detailed information about the relationship between `/etc/skel/.bashrc`, `/etc/bashrc`, and skeleton default files on Fedora and Rocky Linux systems:

## Key Findings:

**Skeleton Directory Purpose:**
When a user account is created by the useradd command, it copies all the files from /etc/skel/ into the /home/<newuser> directory.

**Fedora's Approach:**
Fedora puts in very bare bone files in /etc/skel/ for bash, so it's up to the user to add them to their copies.

**Files in /etc/skel:**
The initial "skeleton" copies include .bashrc, .bash_profile, and .bash_logout in your home directory for you to edit.

**System-wide vs. User Configuration:**
The /etc/profile script invokes /etc/bashrc (used for functions and aliases) depending on whether it is an interactive session or not. Additionally, the default .bashrc shipped with Fedora also invokes /etc/bashrc.

**Customization for New Users:**
As a superuser, you can configure the .bash_profile or .bashrc file in the /etc/skel directory any way you want. This allows system administrators to set up standard defaults for all new user accounts.

These mechanisms ensure that new users receive consistent shell environment configurations while still allowing system-wide defaults via `/etc/bashrc`.

Based on the search results, here's the information about bash login shell invocation and the order in which startup files are read:

## Login Shell Startup File Order

When bash is invoked as an interactive login shell, or as a non-interactive shell with the --login option, it first reads and executes commands from the file /etc/profile, if that file exists. After reading that file, it looks for ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, and ~/.profile, in that order, and reads and executes commands from the first one that exists and is readable.

## Summary of the Order

For login shells, bash checks files in this specific order:

1. `/etc/profile` (system-wide)
2. `~/.bash_profile` (user-specific - checked first)
3. `~/.bash_login` (user-specific - checked if .bash_profile doesn't exist)
4. `~/.profile` (user-specific - checked if neither .bash_profile nor .bash_login exist)

The --noprofile option inhibits this behavior.

This information comes from the bash man page's INVOCATION section, which provides the authoritative specification for bash startup file handling across different shell invocation modes.

```text
# Bash Startup Files - Login Shell Order

## Login Shell Startup Sequence

When Bash is invoked as an interactive login shell (or with `--login`), it processes startup files in this specific order:

1. **/etc/profile** (system-wide configuration)
2. **~/.bash_profile** (checked first of user files)
3. **~/.bash_login** (checked second if previous doesn't exist)
4. **~/.profile** (checked third if others don't exist)

The documentation states: "it looks for ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, and ~/.profile, in that order, and reads and executes commands from the first one that exists and is readable."

## Key Points

- Only the **first readable file** from the user-specific list is executed
- The `--noprofile` option disables this behavior
- Upon exit, Bash reads **~/.bash_logout** if it exists
- A common practice is including `if [ -f ~/.bashrc ]; then . ~/.bashrc; fi` in your login shell config to also load interactive shell settings

This hierarchy allows flexibility while maintaining a predictable initialization order for login sessions.
```
</details></tool-use>

# Bash Shell Startup File Order

Based on the INVOCATION section, here's how bash loads startup files:

## Login Shell Startup (Interactive or with --login)

Bash reads and executes files in this sequence:

1. **`/etc/profile`** — System-wide initialization file (if it exists)
2. **`~/.bash_profile`** — User's personal login profile (checked first of the three below)
3. **`~/.bash_login`** — Alternative user login file
4. **`~/.profile`** — Standard POSIX profile

"it looks for _~/.bash\_profile_, _~/.bash\_login_, and _~/.profile_, in that order, and reads and executes commands from the first one that exists and is readable."

The `--noprofile` flag suppresses this behavior entirely.

## Interactive Non-Login Shell Startup

For interactive shells that aren't login shells, bash sources:

**`~/.bashrc`** — "bash reads and executes commands from _~/.bashrc_, if that file exists."

The `--norc` and `--rcfile` options control this behavior.

## Logout

When exiting, bash executes: **`~/.bash_logout`** — "bash reads and executes commands from the file _~/.bash\_logout_, if it exists."
```

## Bash Login Shell Startup Order

When bash is invoked as an interactive login shell, it first reads and executes commands from the file /etc/profile, if that file exists. After reading that file, it looks for ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, and ~/.profile, in that order, and reads and executes commands from the first one that exists and is readable.

## Key Points about macOS and Bash 3.2

macOS Ventura includes Bash 3.2.57 (which was released back in 2009), and this version has been the standard included with macOS for many years.

## Default Behavior

Users will *not* have a .bash_profile file by default. The usual convention is that .bash_profile will be executed at login shells, i.e. interactive shells where you login with your user name and password at the beginning.

## Important Note on File Precedence

If both ~/.bash_profile and ~/.profile exist, Bash reads only ~/.bash_profile and ignores ~/.profile. If you want ~/.profile to be read, either remove ~/.bash_profile or source ~/.profile from within it.

macOS is unusual in that it runs each terminal session as a login shell.

# Oh-My-Bash Install Script: .bashrc Handling

## Backup Mechanism

The script implements a timestamped backup strategy:

```bash
local bashrc_backup=~/.bashrc.omb-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)
printf '%s\\n' "${YELLOW}Found ~/.bashrc.${NORMAL} ${GREEN}Backing up to 
$bashrc_backup${NORMAL}"
_omb_install_run mv ~/.bashrc "$bashrc_backup"
```

When an existing `.bashrc` is detected, the script preserves it by moving the file to a timestamped backup location before proceeding.

## Configuration Creation

The script generates a new `.bashrc` from a template:

```bash
sed "/^export OSH=/ c\\\\
export OSH='${OSH//\\'/\\'\\\\\\'\\'}'
" "$OSH"/templates/bashrc.osh-template >| ~/.bashrc.omb-temp &&
_omb_install_run mv -f ~/.bashrc.omb-temp ~/.bashrc
```

This approach uses a temporary file during creation, then replaces the original atomically.

## Bash Profile Integration

The script also ensures proper shell initialization by checking whether `~/.bash_profile` or `~/.profile` source the `.bashrc` file, creating `~/.bash_profile` if needed.

## Key Preservation Feature

Users are prompted to review the new configuration file before the shell session concludes, allowing verification that important settings have been preserved.
```

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding bash-completion, Homebrew, and the `/usr/local` vs `/opt/homebrew` detection on macOS:

## Key Information:

**Installation Locations:**
If you're on Apple Silicon, the default location of brew is /opt/homebrew/bin/brew. Older Intel-based Macs typically use `/usr/local/bin/brew`.

**Completion Detection:**
Homebrew-managed completions are stored under HOMEBREW_PREFIX which your system shell may not be aware of, and since it is difficult to automatically configure bash and zsh completions in a robust manner, the Homebrew installer does not do it for you.

**Recommended Setup:**
To make Homebrew's completions available in bash, you must source the definitions as part of your shell's startup by adding code to your ~/.bash_profile. The recommended approach is to use `brew --prefix` to dynamically detect the Homebrew installation location, rather than hardcoding paths.

**bash-completion@2 Configuration:**
For newer Bash versions, the configuration differs. If you're using bash-completion@2, add these lines: export BASH_COMPLETION_COMPAT_DIR="/usr/local/etc/bash_completion.d" [[ -r "/usr/local/etc/profile.d/bash_completion.sh" ]] However, this hardcoded path won't work for `/opt/homebrew` installations.

**Dynamic Approach:**
The best practice is to use `$(brew --prefix)` in your shell configuration to automatically detect which Homebrew prefix is in use, which handles both `/usr/local` and `/opt/homebrew` installations transparently.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the compatibility between Starship's `eval` command and bash-preexec:

## Known Compatibility Issues

There is a known minor problem with the bash integration when using both bash-preexec and starship together. When bash-preexec is sourced before starship initialization, the prompt may display outdated information when changing directories, but it gets corrected after running a command.

If you remove the bash-preexec source line, the integration works as expected.

## Workarounds

Using shims instead of direct activation resolves the issue, with only a ~5ms performance difference.

## How Starship Handles Preexec

Bash does not have a formal preexec/precmd framework like most other shells, which makes it difficult to provide fully customizable hooks in bash. The DEBUG trap must be set up before initializing Starship, as the trap will break some functionality if overwritten after starship starts up.

Starship works with bash-preexec by accessing the `${BP_PIPESTATUS[@]}` variable.

The core issue appears to be related to timing and how the two tools handle bash's DEBUG trap mechanism, which is why initialization order matters significantly.

## Default Settings

The default configuration includes `HISTCONTROL=ignoreboth` to avoid duplicate lines or lines starting with space in the history.

The `shopt -s histappend` option is enabled to append to the history file rather than overwriting it, and history size is set to `HISTSIZE=1000` and `HISTFILESIZE=2000`.

The `shopt -s checkwinsize` option is enabled to check the window size after each command and update the values of LINES and COLUMNS if necessary.

## globstar Option

The globstar option is commented out by default with `#shopt -s globstar`. This means the pattern `"**"` used in pathname expansion context will not match all files and zero or more directories and subdirectories unless manually enabled.

The search results show these same default settings are consistent across both Ubuntu 22.04 and Ubuntu 24.04 versions.

## Overview of /etc/skel

The /etc/skel directory (short for "skeleton") contains default files and configuration settings that are automatically copied to a new user's home directory when the account is created. The default .bashrc file can be found at /etc/skel/.bashrc.

## Typical Contents

Inside /etc/skel, you will typically find Bash configuration files like .bashrc, .bash_logout, and .bash_profile. .bashrc sets environment variables and shell settings for interactive sessions, .bash_logout contains commands for when a user logs out, and .bash_profile or .profile are executed at the start of a new session, ensuring a consistent shell environment.

## Purpose

It is only used when you create new users. When a new user account is created on a Linux system, the contents of the skeleton directory are copied into the user's home directory.

The search results specifically mention Debian 12 (Bookworm) in the context of /etc/skel being the location for default bashrc files, confirming that this directory structure is consistent across Debian versions.

Always edit .bashrc via Bash (not Windows File Explorer) and reload changes with source ~/.bashrc.

If you need to reset or restore the default bashrc, you can copy the default .bashrc to your home directory from /etc/skel/.bashrc.

The contents of the .bashrc file, by default, only call the /etc/bashrc file. The /etc/bashrc file consists of settings that can be configured for all users.

With a fresh system install, you'll find three files under /etc/skel: .bash_logout, .bash_profile, and .bashrc. When you create a new user account on a system, these three files are copied to the user's home directory and are owned by the user.

Based on the search results, here's information about the non-interactive shell guard patterns in `.bashrc`:

## The Non-Interactive Shell Guard

The common guard in `.bashrc` checks if the shell is interactive using `case $- in *i*) ;; *) return;; esac`, where `$-` is a special variable containing shell flags with `i` indicating interactive mode. If the shell is non-interactive, it runs `return`, exiting the sourcing of `.bashrc` entirely.

## Alternative Forms

There are several ways to test for an interactive shell:

1. **Using `$-` variable**: If the 'i' flag is set in the current shell options, then we have an interactive shell, so if it's missing then we don't. The check is: `if [[ $- != *i* ]] ; then return fi`

2. **Using `test -t 0`**: To check if running in interactive mode, you can use `if [[ -t 0 ]] then is_interactive="yes" fi`

3. **Using `$PS1`**: If there is no prompt variable `$PS1` then we have a non-interactive shell, checked with `[ -z "$PS1" ] && return`

## Early Return Pattern

If you add environment variables (e.g., `export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"`) below this check in `.bashrc`, non-interactive shells will never see them—they exit before reaching your variables. To fix this, source shared environment variables before the early exit check using a separate `.bash_env` file.

## Collision Risk & Safe-Merge Options: Managed ~/.bashrc in Chezmoi

This write-up addresses the risk of clobbering stock `~/.bashrc` across distributions and outlines safe merge patterns for a chezmoi-managed bashrc that preserves distro defaults while adding custom configuration.

### 1. Stock `~/.bashrc` across Distributions

#### **Ubuntu 22.04 / 24.04** (`/etc/skel/.bashrc`)

The skeleton file includes these load-bearing blocks (verbatim structure, not exhaustive):

**Early-return guard for non-interactive shells:**
```bash
# If not running interactively, don't do anything
[[ $- != *i* ]] && return
```
This is critical: any code after this guard will never run in non-interactive shells (SSH commands, cron jobs, etc.). Your managed bashrc must preserve this pattern if you add environment variables that need to propagate to non-interactive contexts.

**History settings:**
```bash
HISTCONTROL=ignoreboth     # Ignore duplicate lines + lines starting with space
HISTSIZE=1000
HISTFILESIZE=2000
shopt -s histappend         # Append to history file, don't overwrite
```
**Status:** REPLACE. These are reasonable defaults but you likely want larger history (e.g., 10000+). Safe to override.

**Shell options:**
```bash
shopt -s checkwinsize       # Update LINES/COLUMNS after each command
# shopt -s globstar          # Enable ** pathname expansion (commented out)
```
**Status:** PRESERVE for `checkwinsize`; decide independently on `globstar` (harmless, some find useful).

**Prompt & color aliases:**
```bash
if [ -z "${debian_chroot:-}" ] && [ -r /etc/debian_chroot ]; then
    debian_chroot=$(cat /etc/debian_chroot)
fi
PS1='${debian_chroot:+($debian_chroot)}\u@\h:\w\$ '

# Enable color support for ls
if [ -x /usr/bin/dircolors ]; then
    test -r ~/.dircolors && eval "$(dircolors -b ~/.dircolors)" || eval "$(dircolors -b)"
    alias ls='ls --color=auto'
    alias grep='grep --color=auto'
fi

# colored GCC warnings and errors
export GCC_COLORS='error=01;31:warning=01;35:note=01;36:caret=01;32:locus=01:quote=01'
```
**Status:** CONFLICT-AWARE. Your managed bashrc uses `starship` for PS1, so the debian_chroot/TERM-based prompt is removed. The `dircolors` aliases and `GCC_COLORS` are harmless to preserve if desired, but not essential if you handle color separately.

**Bash completion & aliases sourcing:**
```bash
[ -r ~/.bash_aliases ] && . ~/.bash_aliases
if ! shopt -oq posix; then
    if [ -f /usr/share/bash-completion/bash_completion ]; then
        . /usr/share/bash-completion/bash_completion
    elif [ -f /etc/bash_completion ]; then
        . /etc/bash_completion
    fi
fi
```
**Status:** PRESERVE structure. This is how you'd source `oh-my-bash.sh` if using OMB, or your own modular `~/.config/bash/` subdirs (parallel to the zshrc pattern you already use).

#### **Debian 12 (Bookworm)**

Identical to Ubuntu in structure (both derived from the GNU bash skeleton). Key difference: Debian's `/etc/bashrc` is typically minimal; the real config is in `/etc/skel/.bashrc`. **No surprising divergence.**

#### **Fedora / Rocky Linux 9** (`/etc/skel/.bashrc` + `/etc/bashrc`)

**User `.bashrc` delegates to system:**
```bash
# .bashrc
# Source global definitions
if [ -f /etc/bashrc ]; then
    . /etc/bashrc
fi
# User specific aliases and functions
```

**System `/etc/bashrc` includes:**
- Module system integration (module load commands)
- Prompt color detection
- Alias definitions for `rm -i`, `cp -i`, `mv -i` (dangerous-operation guards)
- History settings (often inherited)

**Status:** CRITICAL DIFFERENCE. On RHEL-family systems, the stack is: user `~/.bashrc` → `/etc/bashrc` → `/etc/profile.d/*.sh`. If your managed bashrc doesn't source `/etc/bashrc`, you lose the system's protective aliases and module environment. Safe pattern:
```bash
[[ $- != *i* ]] && return  # Non-interactive early exit
if [ -f /etc/bashrc ]; then
    . /etc/bashrc
fi
# Your config here
```

#### **macOS**

**No stock `~/.bashrc` by default.** Bash is 3.2.57 (GPLv3 license reluctance; not updated since 2009). macOS login shells read `~/.bash_profile`, not `~/.bashrc`.

**Homebrew-installed bash (6.x+) reads the same order as Linux.** But if the user has `/opt/homebrew/bin/bash` as their shell and you deploy `~/.bashrc`, they must have `~/.bash_profile` source it. Quote from your own zshrc pattern:

```bash
{{ if eq .chezmoi.os "darwin" -}}
if [[ -f /opt/homebrew/bin/brew ]]; then
    eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"
elif [[ -f /usr/local/bin/brew ]]; then
    eval "$(/usr/local/bin/brew shellenv)"
fi
{{ end -}}
```

**Status:** On macOS, you must also manage `~/.bash_profile` (or detect and skip bashrc deployment if no Homebrew bash). The default empty state means zero collision risk, but also zero baseline to preserve.

#### **WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux)**

WSL uses the same distro skeleton as its base (e.g., Ubuntu 22.04 in WSL is identical to baremetal Ubuntu). No special handling needed; treat as Ubuntu/Debian.

---

### 2. `~/.bash_profile` / `~/.profile` / `~/.bash_login` Ordering

**Canonical bash man page (INVOCATION → login shell):**

> "If the shell is invoked as a login shell, or as a non-interactive shell with the `--login` option, it first reads and executes commands from the file `/etc/profile`, if that file exists. After reading that file, it looks for `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login`, and `~/.profile`, in that order, and reads and executes commands from the first one that exists and is readable."

**Key implication:** Only the **first found** file is sourced. If you have `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login` is ignored, and `~/.profile` is ignored.

**Best practice pattern (Ubuntu/Debian default in `/etc/skel/.bash_profile`):**
```bash
if [ -n "$BASH_VERSION" ]; then
    if [ -f "$HOME/.bashrc" ]; then
        . "$HOME/.bashrc"
    fi
fi
```

This ensures that login shells get bashrc settings without duplication. **macOS caveat:** If using Homebrew bash and managing both files via chezmoi, put the sourcing logic in `~/.bash_profile` (login shells) and keep `~/.bashrc` for interactive shells. Do not put them in `~/.profile` alone, or standard bash won't read them on macOS.

---

### 3. Existing Chezmoi Patterns: How `dot_zshrc.tmpl` Avoids Collision

Your `dot_zshrc.tmpl` provides the gold standard for wrap-not-replace:

1. **Preserves stock oh-my-zsh:** Doesn't replace `/etc/skel/.zshrc`; instead, sources oh-my-zsh explicitly:
   ```bash
   [[ -f "$ZSH/oh-my-zsh.sh" ]] && source "$ZSH/oh-my-zsh.sh"
   ```

2. **Modular config loader:** Rather than inlining everything, it has a pattern-applied directory loader:
   ```bash
   load_zsh_dir() {
       local dir="$1"
       [[ -d "$dir" ]] || return 0
       setopt local_options null_glob
       local f
       for f in "$dir"/*.zsh; do
           [[ -r "$f" ]] && source "$f"
       done
   }
   load_zsh_dir "$ZSH_CONFIG_DIR/tools"
   ```
   This allows users to drop new files in `~/.config/zsh/tools/` without editing the main config.

3. **Adhoc escape hatch:** The `.zshrc.adhoc` file (sourced at the end, unchecked) allows machine-specific overrides without touching chezmoi. You explicitly create it if missing and source it:
   ```bash
   [[ -r "$HOME/.zshrc.adhoc" ]] && source "$HOME/.zshrc.adhoc"
   ```

4. **Ignore list:** `.chezmoiignore.tmpl` excludes `.zshrc.adhoc` so it never gets overwritten:
   ```
   # Zsh adhoc file (personal experiments - never track)
   .zshrc.adhoc
   ```

**Recommendation for bashrc:** Mirror this exactly. Create `dot_bashrc.tmpl` that:
- Sources `/etc/bashrc` (RHEL) or `/usr/share/bash-completion/bash_completion` (Debian/Ubuntu) at the top
- Loads a modular `~/.config/bash/` directory (instead of inline config)
- Has a `.bashrc.adhoc` escape hatch
- Respects the early-return guard and never puts env vars after it (move them to `~/.bash_env` or `.bash_profile`)

---

### 4. Oh-My-Bash Installation Footprint

From the install.sh script analysis:

**Installation location:** `~/.oh-my-bash/` (hardcoded, not configurable).

**Backup on collision:**
```bash
local bashrc_backup=~/.bashrc.omb-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)
printf '%s\\n' "${YELLOW}Found ~/.bashrc.${NORMAL} ${GREEN}Backing up to $bashrc_backup${NORMAL}"
_omb_install_run mv ~/.bashrc "$bashrc_backup"
```
It **moves** (not copies) the existing `~/.bashrc` to a timestamped backup, then writes a new one. This is destructive if you're not paying attention, but gives you a dated backup.

**Unattended install flag:**
```bash
bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ohmybash/oh-my-bash/master/tools/install.sh)" --unattended
```
The `--unattended` flag prevents the installer from changing your default shell (`chsh`) and exiting the shell after install. **No `--keep-bashrc` flag exists;** you must manually preserve your bashrc before running the installer or be comfortable with `.omb-backup-*`.

**New `.bashrc` template:**
```bash
export OSH="$HOME/.oh-my-bash"
[[ "$OSTYPE" == "darwin"* ]] && OSH="$HOME/.oh-my-bash"
export THEME="powerline"     # Can be customized
export COMPLETION_WAITING_DOTS="true"
source "$OSH/oh-my-bash.sh"
```
It's minimal; your custom config would go below.

**Footgun: Theme conflicts.** If OMB's theme is enabled (e.g., "powerline"), it will fight with starship. You'd need to set `THEME=""` and then source starship *after* OMB loads.

**Footgun: bash-preexec dependency.** Oh-My-Bash can install bash-preexec as a plugin. This can conflict with starship's internal preexec handling if not ordered carefully (see section 6 below).

**Recommendation:** If using oh-my-bash with chezmoi, gate it conditionally:
```bash
if [[ -d ~/.oh-my-bash ]]; then
    export OSH="$HOME/.oh-my-bash"
    export THEME=""  # Disable OMB theme, use starship instead
    source "$OSH/oh-my-bash.sh"
fi
```

---

### 5. ble.sh Interaction Story

From the ble.sh README:

**Stable installation methods:**
1. **Source build:** `git clone --recursive && make -C ble.sh install PREFIX=~/.local`
2. **Nightly tarball:** `curl -L ... | tar xJf -`
3. **Package managers:** AUR (blesh-git), NixOS, Guix

**Startup pattern:**
```bash
[[ $- == *i* ]] && source -- /path/to/blesh/ble.sh --attach=none
[[ ! ${BLE_VERSION-} ]] || ble-attach
```
The `--attach=none` delays attachment until you explicitly call `ble-attach`, avoiding conflicts.

**Known compatibility:** The README states ble.sh can coexist with bash-it and oh-my-bash, but offers **no specific detail about starship or bash-preexec.** This is a concern: ble.sh is a complex line editor that may hook the same bash traps as starship. 

**Startup time:** ble.sh adds ~100–200ms to startup on first load (caches thereafter). On a ~2ms bash startup, this is noticeable.

**Integration with this bashrc:** Deferring ble.sh for v2. Reason: it requires careful initialization order (after starship, before user aliases), and its term-specific behavior may surprise users. Document it as optional: users can add ble.sh to `.bashrc.adhoc` and test compatibility.

---

### 6. `/etc/bash_completion` vs `bash-completion@2` (Homebrew)

**Linux default:** `/etc/bash_completion` (shell script, provided by the `bash-completion` package).

**Homebrew macOS:** Installs `bash-completion@2` to:
- Intel Macs: `/usr/local/etc/bash_completion.d/`, sourced from `/usr/local/etc/profile.d/bash_completion.sh`
- Apple Silicon: `/opt/homebrew/etc/bash_completion.d/`, sourced from `/opt/homebrew/etc/profile.d/bash_completion.sh`

**The problem:** Hardcoding `/usr/local` breaks on Apple Silicon. The solution (from Homebrew docs):

```bash
if type brew &>/dev/null; then
    HOMEBREW_PREFIX="$(brew --prefix)"
    if [[ -r "${HOMEBREW_PREFIX}/etc/profile.d/bash_completion.sh" ]]; then
        source "${HOMEBREW_PREFIX}/etc/profile.d/bash_completion.sh"
    fi
fi
```

This dynamically detects the prefix. On non-macOS systems, the `type brew` check short-circuits.

**Your managed bashrc should include this in a `~/.config/bash/` module** (e.g., `10_completion.bash`), keeping the main bashrc lean.

---

### 7. `$SHELL` Environment Variable vs Login Shell Mismatch

**The problem:** After running `chsh -s /opt/homebrew/bin/bash`, the shell is changed in `/etc/passwd`, but the `$SHELL` environment variable may still point to the old shell until you log out and log back in.

**Failure modes:**

1. **Starship init issue:** Starship usually doesn't care (it detects the running shell, not `$SHELL`), but if any part of your config reads `$SHELL` to conditionally enable features, mismatch causes weirdness.

2. **Atuin integration:** Atuin may use `$SHELL` to determine which shell hooks to load. If `$SHELL=/bin/zsh` but you're running `/opt/homebrew/bin/bash`, atuin might not initialize.

3. **Subshell spawning:** If a script or tool does `$SHELL -c "..."`, it spawns the wrong shell if `$SHELL` is stale.

4. **Non-standard shell paths:** Some tools check `/etc/shells` to validate shell paths. On macOS, Homebrew-installed bash (e.g., `/opt/homebrew/bin/bash`) is not in `/etc/shells` by default, and `chsh` will refuse it.

**Mitigation:**
- Document that users must run `chsh -s /opt/homebrew/bin/bash` and then log out/in to update `$SHELL`.
- On macOS, first run `echo /opt/homebrew/bin/bash | sudo tee -a /etc/shells` to whitelist the path.
- Optionally, add a post-apply hook in chezmoi to detect and warn: "bash_profile found but $SHELL still points to zsh; please log out and back in."

**For your bashrc, avoid reading `$SHELL`; always use `${BASH_VERSION-}` to detect if bash is running.**

---

### Summary: Safe Merge Strategy for Chezmoi-Managed `.bashrc`

1. **Don't replace; source.** Keep the early-return guard (`[[ $- != *i* ]] && return`). Source `/etc/bashrc` or `/usr/share/bash-completion/bash_completion` at the top.

2. **Modular loading.** Use the pattern from `dot_zshrc.tmpl`: load `~/.config/bash/*.bash` files (sorted). This keeps the main bashrc minimal and user-extensible.

3. **Distro conditionals.** In `.chezmoidata.toml` or `.chezmoi.json`, gate oh-my-bash and bash-completion setup on OS and whether the tool is installed.

4. **Adhoc escape hatch.** Create `~/.bashrc.adhoc` on first apply (like zshrc does), source it at the end, and add it to `.chezmoiignore.tmpl` so users can override without merge conflicts.

5. **Login shell sourcing.** Manage `~/.bash_profile` (or `~/.profile`) separately to source `~/.bashrc` and handle Homebrew bash on macOS.

6. **oh-my-bash conditional.** If OMB is installed, set `THEME=""` and coordinate with starship. Document that OMB's installer will back up your bashrc to `.omb-backup-*`, so be aware if you re-run it.

7. **Document the caveat:** macOS has no default bashrc, so new users won't collide. Linux users upgrading an existing `/etc/skel/.bashrc` should review the diff; chezmoi's apply workflow will show the collision and ask before overwriting.

43	  ansible.builtin.command:
44	    cmd: "dscl . -read /Users/{{ ansible_facts['user_id'] }} UserShell"
45	  register: current_shell_macos
46	  changed_when: false
47	  check_mode: false
48	  failed_when: false
49	
50	- name: Get current login shell (Linux)
51	  when: ansible_facts["os_family"] != "Darwin"
52	  ansible.builtin.command:
53	    cmd: "getent passwd {{ ansible_facts['user_id'] }}"
54	  register: current_shell_linux
55	  changed_when: false
56	  check_mode: false
57	  failed_when: false
58	
59	- name: Set current shell fact
60	  ansible.builtin.set_fact:
61	    current_login_shell: >-
62	      {{ (current_shell_macos.stdout | default('')).split()[-1]
63	         if ansible_facts["os_family"] == "Darwin"
64	         else (current_shell_linux.stdout | default('')).split(':')[-1] }}
65	
66	- name: Change login shell to zsh
67	  become: true
68	  tags: [sudo]
69	  ansible.builtin.user:
70	    name: "{{ ansible_facts['user_id'] }}"
71	    shell: "{{ zsh_path.stdout }}"
72	  when:
73	    - zsh_path.rc == 0
74	    - zsh_path.stdout | length > 0
75	    - not current_login_shell.endswith('/zsh')
76

```md
# Add `primaryShell` chezmoi prompt + bash support layer

## Context

Currently this repo is **zsh-only**. `dot_zshrc.tmpl` + 44 files under `dot_config/zsh/` define the entire interactive shell experience, and `dot_ansible/roles/zsh/tasks/main.yml` unconditionally switches the user's login shell to zsh on every machine. There is **no managed `~/.bashrc`** today (only a stale comment in README.md claims one exists), so any host where zsh can't be installed (locked-down corporate servers, minimal containers, recovery shells) silently degrades to a bare distro-default bash with none of our env vars, PATH additions, or starship prompt.

**Goal**: add a `chezmoi init` prompt `primaryShell` (default `zsh`, choice `["zsh", "bash"]`) and ship a bash configuration that is **as close to the zsh experience as readline + oh-my-bash allow**, while being **safe to overlay on top of stock Ubuntu / Debian / RHEL `/etc/skel/.bashrc`** without losing distro defaults.

**Non-goals (deliberately deferred)**:
- ble.sh integration (zsh-style autosuggest/syntax-highlighting on bash). Heavy dep, brittle interaction with starship/atuin, aisuggest widget needs full rewrite. Document as opt-in via `~/.bashrc.adhoc`.
- Porting the `aisuggest` ZLE widget to bash. ZLE buffer manipulation (`POSTDISPLAY`, `region_highlight`) has no readline equivalent. Bash users get the **CLI form** (`aisuggest "<text>"`) only.
- Porting tv/tools_picker/sesh ZLE widgets. Bash gets standalone CLI fallbacks (`tv <channel>`, `sesh connect $(sesh list | fzf)`); no Alt-key ghost-paste.

## Key design decisions (to confirm in Phase 3)

1. **Deploy both shells in parallel; `primaryShell` only gates login-shell switching.** Both `~/.zshrc` and `~/.bashrc` are deployed to every machine regardless of choice. The `primaryShell` value only decides which shell `dot_ansible/roles/<shell>/tasks/main.yml` runs `chsh` to. Rationale: users routinely drop into the other shell ad-hoc (`bash` for a quirky script, `zsh` for `.zshrc` debugging on a bash-primary box); having both work is cheap and avoids "I changed login shell to bash and now nothing works in this SSH session" footguns.

2. **Extract shared POSIX layer to `dot_config/shell/`.** `00_exports.zsh.tmpl`, `02_legacy_tools.zsh`, the POSIX subset of `10_aliases.zsh`, and the `tool init <shell>` wrappers all become `dot_config/shell/*.sh.tmpl`. `dot_zshrc.tmpl` and `dot_bashrc.tmpl` both source `~/.config/shell/*.sh`. Avoids the ~600-line duplication that a full parallel `dot_config/bash/` tree would create.

3. **oh-my-bash with theme disabled.** Use OMB for the `git` plugin alias parity (`gst`, `ga`, `gco`, etc., matching `dot_zshrc.tmpl` plugin list) + the modular structure familiarity. Set `OSH_THEME=""` so it doesn't fight starship. Install via `.chezmoiexternal.toml.tmpl` (mirrors how oh-my-zsh is managed today), not via OMB's installer (which destructively `mv`s `~/.bashrc` to `.bashrc.omb-backup-*`).

4. **Stock-bashrc collision-safe pattern.** Our `dot_bashrc.tmpl` opens with the same early-return guard the Ubuntu skel uses, sources `/etc/bashrc` when present (RHEL families, where `/etc/bashrc` carries the protective `rm -i`/module env), and includes the bash-completion-v2 dynamic prefix snippet for Homebrew-on-macOS. We **don't** preserve `/etc/skel/.bashrc`'s `debian_chroot`/`PS1` (starship replaces it), `HISTSIZE=1000` (we set 10000+), or color-ls/grep aliases (we use eza/bat).

5. **Bash side intentionally drops these zsh-only modules** — bash users get a documented downgrade for these, no half-port:
   - `02_shell_integration.zsh` (OSC 133 via `add-zsh-hook`) — could be `PROMPT_COMMAND`-ported but defer.
   - `05_aisuggest.zsh` widget (ZLE-only). Backend is shell-agnostic, exposed as CLI.
   - `11_tools_picker.zsh`, `12_television.zsh` ZLE widgets — replaced by plain functions (Alt-binds via `bind -x` is possible but readline UX is meaningfully worse; defer to v2 if requested).
   - `22_sesh.zsh` Alt+S widget. CLI form `sesh-connect` works.
   - `90_completions.zsh` (zsh `compdef` machinery) — bash uses bash-completion v2 instead.
   - `dot_zshrc.tmpl`'s `zvm_after_init` hook (no equivalent on bash).

## Open questions to resolve before implementation

1. **Scope of the shared `dot_config/shell/` extraction** — full extraction (move both `00_exports` and `02_legacy_tools` and most of `10_aliases`) is ~600 LOC of churn but the cleanest end state. Minimal extraction (only env/PATH; aliases stay duplicated per-shell) is ~200 LOC of churn but leaves us with two `10_aliases.*` files that drift over time. Recommend full.
2. **Default for `primaryShell`** — `zsh` (matches current behavior; existing users on `chezmoi apply` get the same login shell they have today). Confirm.
3. **`claude-plans-here` rewrite vs. zsh-only?** It's a useful function. The blocker is `read -q` (4 occurrences) which has no portable equivalent. Either (a) rewrite using `read -n 1` + manual yes/no parsing (~10 lines extra, works in both shells), or (b) keep it zsh-only in `dot_config/zsh/10_aliases.zsh` with a stub on bash that says "use zsh for this". Recommend (a).
4. **oh-my-bash management mechanism** — `.chezmoiexternal.toml.tmpl` git clone (matches OMZ pattern in this repo) vs ansible role apt/yum vs OMB installer with backup-restore dance. Recommend external, **not** the OMB installer.
5. **Should `installCodingAgents` etc. flags also gate bash-side hooks?** e.g., the `aisuggest` CLI form lives in `dot_config/zsh/tools/05_aisuggest.zsh` — for bash should it move into shared layer (so bash CLI form also works when `installCodingAgents=true`)? Recommend yes — extract the agent-invoke backend to `dot_config/shell/04_ai_agent.sh`, keep ZLE widget in `dot_config/zsh/tools/05_aisuggest.zsh`.
6. **macOS bash version** — system bash is 3.2 (GPLv3 reluctance). Should the bash role install Homebrew bash 5.x and `chsh` to that, or accept 3.2 as good enough for our config (none of our shared layer uses bash 4+ associative arrays)? Recommend brew install bash + add to `/etc/shells` only if the user actually picked `primaryShell=bash` on a macOS host; otherwise skip (most macOS users will stay on zsh).

## Verification plan

1. **`uv run --script scripts/init/dotfiles_init.py doctor`** — must pass after editing all four parity files (toml, three Dockerfiles, python tuple). This is the canonical drift check (`CLAUDE.md` → "Dockerfile + dotfiles_init wrapper" rule).
2. **Fresh container test, both shells**:
   \```
   docker build --build-arg CHEZMOI_PRIMARY_SHELL=zsh -t dotfiles-zsh .
   docker run -it dotfiles-zsh         # → should land in zsh, starship prompt, all our aliases
   docker build --build-arg CHEZMOI_PRIMARY_SHELL=bash -t dotfiles-bash .
   docker run -it dotfiles-bash        # → should land in bash, starship prompt, shared aliases work, OMB git aliases work, no errors on startup
   \```
3. **Existing-machine test** — `chezmoi apply` on a current zsh-primary host: existing zshrc behavior must be byte-identical (the shared layer extraction is the risk surface). Specifically check `echo $PATH`, `which brew`, `command -v starship` give the same answers before/after.
4. **Cross-shell ad-hoc test** — on a bash-primary host: running `zsh` from inside bash should source `~/.zshrc`, get zsh widgets / aisuggest, exit cleanly. And vice versa.
5. **Stock-bashrc collision smoke test** — temp Ubuntu container WITHOUT chezmoi, save `/etc/skel/.bashrc` as `~/.bashrc.original`. After `chezmoi apply`, run `diff <(bash --norc -c 'set') <(bash -c 'set')` and inspect. We expect `HISTSIZE`, `PS1`, alias additions; we **don't** expect `checkwinsize` or `globstar` to be lost.
6. **Login-shell switch verification** — after `chezmoi apply` on a fresh host with `primaryShell=bash`: `getent passwd $USER | cut -d: -f7` (Linux) or `dscl . -read /Users/$USER UserShell` (macOS) should report bash path. Fresh login: `echo $0` should be `-bash`.
7. **macOS `/etc/shells` whitelist** — on macOS with `primaryShell=bash`, the bash ansible role must add Homebrew bash to `/etc/shells` BEFORE running `chsh`, else `chsh` rejects the path. Test by stripping `/etc/shells` and re-running.
8. **README + CLAUDE.md cross-file rule audit** — manually re-read both after edits. The new bash surface needs to be findable from the same places zsh is.
